lessons.title: ARC & Retain Counts
lessons.body:
Swift uses **Automatic Reference Counting (ARC)** to manage memory. The compiler analyzes your code at compile time and automatically inserts `retain` and `release` calls — you never write them yourself.

Every class instance has an internal **retain count**. When you create an instance, the count starts at 1. Each new strong reference increments it; each reference going away decrements it. When the count reaches **0**, ARC immediately calls `deinit` and frees the memory.

```swift
class Car {
    let model: String
    init(_ model: String) { self.model = model }
    deinit { print("\(model) deallocated") }
}

var first: Car? = Car("Tesla")  // retain count = 1
var second: Car? = first         // retain count = 2
first = nil                      // retain count = 1
second = nil                     // retain count = 0 → deinit called
```

This is fundamentally different from **garbage collection** (used by Java or Go). A garbage collector runs periodically on a separate thread and cleans up unreachable objects in batches — timing is non-deterministic. ARC is **deterministic**: deallocation happens the instant the last reference disappears, making resource cleanup predictable and tight.

Because ARC works at compile time rather than runtime, there is no GC pause or background scan. The trade-off is that ARC cannot automatically detect **retain cycles**, which you must handle yourself with `weak` and `unowned` references.

quickCheck.prompt: When does ARC call deinit on an object?
quickCheck.explanation: ARC tracks the retain count for every class instance. The moment that count reaches 0 — meaning no strong references remain — ARC immediately calls deinit and frees the memory.

options.text: When retain count drops to 0
When the app moves to background
After every function returns
At the end of the run loop

lessons.title: strong, weak, and unowned

quickCheck.prompt: What type must a `weak` variable be?
quickCheck.explanation: ARC automatically zeroes a weak reference when its target is deallocated. Optional is the correct type because the value can legitimately become nil at any point without programmer intervention.

options.text: Optional
non-Optional
AnyObject
Any

lessons.title: Retain Cycles & Closures

quickCheck.prompt: In a closure capture list, `[weak self]` makes self…
quickCheck.explanation: Capturing self as weak gives it Optional type inside the closure, allowing ARC to nil it out if the object is deallocated before the closure runs — preventing both a cycle and a crash.

options.text: Optional inside the closure
unowned
a strong reference
nil immediately

lessons.title: Leak Patterns, Autorelease Pools & Debugging Tools
lessons.body:
Beyond simple two-object cycles, several everyday APIs create leaks in ways that are easy to miss. `Timer.scheduledTimer(target:)` retains its target strongly — a repeating timer on `self` keeps `self` alive as long as the timer is scheduled, and if `self` also holds the timer in a property, neither side is ever released.

```swift
class ReportViewController: UIViewController {
    weak var timer: Timer?  // storing it weakly doesn't fix the cycle by itself

    override func viewWillDisappear(_ animated: Bool) {
        super.viewWillDisappear(animated)
        timer?.invalidate()  // break the cycle explicitly — don't rely on deinit
    }
}
```

The fix has to be proactive: call `invalidate()` from a lifecycle method like `viewWillDisappear`, not from `deinit` — if the timer is what's keeping the view controller alive, `deinit` will never run to invalidate it.

`NotificationCenter` observers used to require an explicit `removeObserver` call in `deinit` to avoid a dangling-pointer crash on the next post. Since iOS 9, the framework holds observers weakly and stops delivering to a deallocated one automatically — the crash risk is gone, though tidying up observers you no longer need is still good hygiene. Delegate properties should almost always be `weak var delegate: SomeDelegate?`: a strong delegate reference is one of the most common accidental cycles, since the delegate typically already owns the object it delegates to.

When memory pressure hits, ARC doesn't proactively free anything extra — it has already freed everything it can prove is unreachable. The tools for finding what's *not* unreachable but shouldn't still be alive are Xcode's **Memory Graph Debugger** (a snapshot of every live object and the reference path keeping it alive) and Instruments' **Allocations** and **Leaks** templates (which track instance counts over time and flag cycles with no incoming root reference).

An `autoreleasepool { }` block is a manual escape hatch: code that produces many autoreleased Objective-C-bridged objects in a tight loop can spike peak memory, because those objects only get freed when the pool drains — normally once per run-loop turn. Wrapping the loop body in its own pool drains far more often, capping the peak instead of letting temporaries accumulate.

quickCheck.prompt: Why can relying on `deinit` to call `timer.invalidate()` fail to ever break a Timer-based retain cycle?
quickCheck.explanation: Timer.scheduledTimer(target:) retains its target strongly. If that same object is what's supposed to invalidate the timer inside deinit, deinit itself never runs — the timer is the very thing keeping the object alive, so the cycle has to be broken from outside (e.g. viewWillDisappear), not from within deinit.

options.text: Because Timer.invalidate() is asynchronous and completes after deinit already ran
Because Timer instances ignore invalidate() calls made specifically from deinit
Because the timer retains the object strongly, so deinit never runs while the cycle exists
Because deinit cannot call methods on self, only read stored properties

questions.prompt: What does ARC stand for, and what problem does it solve?
questions.explanation: ARC (Automatic Reference Counting) is a compile-time mechanism: the compiler inserts retain and release calls for you based on static analysis of ownership, so you don't track object lifetimes by hand.

options.text: Automatic Reference Counting — the compiler inserts retain/release calls based on static analysis of ownership
Adaptive Runtime Cache — a background thread periodically scans for unreachable objects and reclaims them, much like a tracing garbage collector
Async Resource Coordinator — a scheduler that defers deallocation until the run loop goes idle
Application Resource Controller — a system service that caps how much memory a process may allocate

questions.prompt: You're deciding between `weak` and `unowned` for a back-reference from a child object to its parent. When is `unowned` the appropriate choice?
questions.explanation: `unowned` skips the Optional wrapper and the nil-check `weak` requires, but it only works safely if the referenced object is guaranteed to outlive the reference; otherwise it crashes rather than degrading gracefully to nil.

options.text: Whenever the reference points at a delegate, since delegates are conventionally unowned
When the child's own lifetime is longer than the parent's
When the referenced object outlives the reference by design
When you want the compiler to insert a nil check automatically before every access

questions.prompt: What happens when this code finishes running?
questions.explanation: a.next holds b strongly and b.next holds a strongly, so each object's retain count stays above zero even after the local variables a and b are set to nil — neither deinit fires and both nodes leak.

options.text: deinit prints twice, once for each node, in the order they were nil'd
deinit never prints — the two nodes hold each other in a retain cycle
deinit prints once, for whichever node was created first
The program crashes because next is still non-nil when the variable is cleared

questions.prompt: A view model stores a closure in a property, and the closure calls a method on `self`. What's the most direct way to prevent this from creating a permanent retain cycle?
questions.explanation: Adding self to the closure's capture list changes how the closure captures it — weakly or unowned — so the closure no longer contributes a strong reference back to the object that owns it.

options.text: Move the closure's body into a separate top-level function so it can't reference self
Mark the property lazy so the closure is created only once
Declare the property static so it isn't tied to a specific instance
Add [weak self] or [unowned self] to the closure's capture list

questions.prompt: What does this print, and in what order?
questions.explanation: `t` is a local variable inside test(); once test() returns, that scope ends and t's only strong reference disappears, so ARC calls deinit before control returns to the caller and "after" is printed.

options.text: gone, then after
after, then gone
gone only — after never prints
Neither prints; the object is deallocated silently since it's unused after assignment

questions.prompt: A junior developer says: "Structs get retain-counted too, just less often than classes." Is this accurate?
questions.explanation: ARC's bookkeeping exists specifically for reference types. Structs and enums are copied by value; there is no shared instance to count references to, so no retain/release traffic happens for them at all.

options.text: Yes — structs are retained once, on first assignment, then never again
Yes, but only for structs that happen to contain at least one class-typed property somewhere inside them
No — ARC only tracks class instances; structs and enums carry no retain count
No — structs use a separate, lighter-weight counting scheme instead of ARC

questions.prompt: Why does Swift require a `weak` reference to be an Optional type?
questions.explanation: When the referenced object is deallocated, ARC has to leave the weak variable pointing at something valid — it zeroes it to nil. Only an Optional type can legally hold that nil.

options.text: Because weak references are always declared with var, and var requires Optional
Because ARC sets the reference to nil automatically once the object is deallocated
Because the Swift compiler cannot resolve the concrete type of a weak reference otherwise
Because weak references are stored differently in memory and require boxing

questions.prompt: A closure captures a view controller with `[unowned self]` and is stored on a singleton that outlives the view controller. What happens when the singleton later invokes the closure?
questions.explanation: unowned assumes its target is still alive at the point of access. If the view controller has already been deallocated by the time the singleton fires the closure, accessing self triggers undefined behavior — typically a crash.

options.text: The closure silently no-ops since self is now nil
ARC extends the view controller's lifetime for as long as the closure itself is retained
The compiler rejects storing an unowned capture on a singleton at build time
Accessing a deallocated unowned reference crashes immediately

questions.prompt: Will "B gone" print after this code runs?
questions.explanation: A's reference to B is weak, so it doesn't count toward B's retain count. Once the local `b` variable is cleared, B has no remaining strong references — including from A — and deinit runs.

options.text: Yes — the weak reference doesn't keep B alive, so it deinitializes normally
No — A and B still form a retain cycle through the two properties
It depends on which variable, a or b, is cleared first
No — B can only deinitialize once A itself deinitializes first

questions.prompt: A property holds an `@escaping` closure that captures `self` with no capture list. Why does this alone create a retain cycle?
questions.explanation: The object owns the closure through its property, and the closure owns the object through the default strong capture of self — each side is the only thing keeping the other one alive, so neither can ever reach a retain count of zero.

options.text: Because @escaping closures are heap-allocated once and never deallocated by ARC
Because the property observer re-captures self on every write
The property retains the closure, and the closure's default capture retains self back — a two-way hold
Because Swift closures always capture their enclosing type twice: once by reference and once by value

questions.prompt: Two variables, `first` and `second`, both point at the same class instance. If you set `first = nil`, what happens to the underlying object?
questions.explanation: The instance's retain count only drops by one strong reference. Since `second` still holds a strong reference, the count stays above zero and the object remains alive.

options.text: It's deallocated immediately, since first was the original owner
Nothing yet — the object stays alive because second still holds a strong reference
It's deallocated the next time the run loop turns over
second becomes nil automatically, mirroring first

questions.prompt: What is an autorelease pool primarily used to manage?
questions.explanation: Some Cocoa/Objective-C APIs return objects marked for deferred release. An autorelease pool batches those deferred releases and drains them at a defined point, rather than releasing each one the instant it goes out of scope.

options.text: Weak references that would otherwise never be zeroed out
Retain cycles created by closures capturing self
Struct copies produced by copy-on-write
Deferred-release objects, drained together

questions.prompt: This helper bridges a Swift object across a C callback boundary. If the opaque pointer is later read with takeUnretainedValue() but release() is never called on it, what happens?
questions.explanation: passRetained bumps the retain count by one, outside of ARC's normal bookkeeping. takeUnretainedValue reads the object without touching that count, so the extra retain from passRetained is never balanced by a matching release — the object leaks for the rest of the process's life.

options.text: The extra retain from passRetained is never balanced, so the object leaks permanently
ARC notices the missing release and inserts one automatically at the next deallocation pass
The object deallocates as soon as read returns, since Unmanaged bypasses ARC entirely
takeUnretainedValue balances the retain internally, so no leak occurs

questions.prompt: A `lazy var` holding a class instance is first accessed inside a method. When is that instance actually created?
questions.explanation: A lazy property's initializer doesn't run at object construction time; it runs the first time the property is read, and the result is cached for every subsequent access.

options.text: At the moment the owning object is initialized, same as any other stored property
Every time the property is read, producing a fresh instance each time
The first time the property is read; the result is then cached for later reads
Only when the app receives a memory warning

questions.prompt: This view controller schedules a repeating timer in viewDidLoad. What's wrong with it?
questions.explanation: Timer.scheduledTimer(target:) retains its target strongly, and the view controller retains the timer back through its property — a cycle. Because the view controller is never deallocated, deinit (and the invalidate() call inside it) never runs, so the timer keeps firing and the strong reference is never broken.

options.text: repeats: true is invalid syntax for a Timer created this way
The timer retains the view controller strongly, so deinit never runs to invalidate it
@objc selectors cannot be used with Timer, only with NotificationCenter
The timer fires only once because scheduledTimer ignores the repeats parameter on the main run loop

questions.prompt: You suspect a screen is leaking after every push/pop cycle. Which Xcode tool is best suited to confirm that an instance count keeps growing instead of returning to a baseline?
questions.explanation: The Memory Graph Debugger snapshots every live object and its reference paths at a point in time, letting you compare instance counts across navigation cycles and trace exactly which reference is keeping a supposedly-dismissed object alive.

options.text: The View Debugger, since it shows the live view hierarchy and every constraint currently applied to it
Console.app, filtered on the app's process name
The Time Profiler, since it samples CPU stack traces
The Memory Graph Debugger, which snapshots live objects and their reference paths

questions.prompt: A class has a stored property that is itself a struct. What does that imply about retain counting for the struct's contents?
questions.explanation: A struct has no retain count of its own — it's copied by value, embedded directly in the class instance's storage. If the struct in turn holds a class property, that inner class reference is what actually gets retained.

options.text: The struct itself is never retained; only any class instances nested inside it are
The struct is retained once and shares that single retain count with the owning class
The struct triggers a second, independent ARC pass separate from the class's own
Storing a struct inside a class always forces a copy-on-write duplication at access time

questions.prompt: A struct has `var friends: [String]`. You copy the struct into a new variable, then append to friends on only the copy. When does the underlying array buffer actually get duplicated?
questions.explanation: Array is copy-on-write: assigning the struct copies the struct's fields, including the array's reference to its buffer, but the underlying storage is shared until a mutation happens. The append call is what detects a shared buffer and triggers the real duplication.

options.text: Immediately when the struct is copied, before any mutation happens
Never — arrays inside structs always share one buffer permanently
At the point of the append call, when Array detects the buffer is shared and copies it first
Only if the array's element count exceeds its current capacity

questions.prompt: This class registers for a notification in init and cleans up in deinit. On a deployment target of iOS 13, is that cleanup call load-bearing?
questions.explanation: Since iOS 9, NotificationCenter holds observers weakly and stops delivering to a deallocated observer automatically, so this particular removeObserver call is redundant rather than required — on older targets it was mandatory to avoid a crash on the next post. It's still harmless and a defensible habit, just not load-bearing here.

options.text: No — on any target, addObserver never retains its observer at all
No — since iOS 9, NotificationCenter holds observers weakly, so that crash risk is gone
Yes — without it, the app crashes the next time .didSync is posted after SyncManager is gone
Yes — SyncManager can't be deallocated at all until removeObserver runs first

questions.prompt: Is a closure a value type or a reference type in Swift?
questions.explanation: Closures capture their environment on the heap and are reference types: assigning a closure to a new variable, or storing the same closure in two properties, shares the identical captured context rather than duplicating it.

options.text: Value type — each assignment copies the captured variables
Neither — closures are a compiler-only construct with no runtime representation
It depends on whether the closure is marked @escaping
Reference type — assigning it shares the same captured context, not a copy

questions.prompt: Two Array<Int> variables currently share the same underlying buffer via copy-on-write. What specifically triggers the actual buffer copy?
questions.explanation: Swift's COW containers check the buffer's reference count immediately before a mutation. If more than one owner holds it, the mutating operation copies the buffer first and applies the change to the new copy; if the count is 1, it mutates in place.

options.text: A mutating operation on one of them, once it detects the buffer is shared
The moment the second variable is assigned from the first
Reading either array's count property
Passing either array as a function argument, regardless of whether the function mutates it

questions.prompt: A protocol used purely as a `weak var` delegate type needs to add `: AnyObject` to its declaration. Why?
questions.explanation: weak only makes sense for reference types, since it relies on ARC's per-instance retain count going to zero. Constraining the protocol to AnyObject rules out struct or enum conformers, which have no retain count for weak to hook into.

options.text: Because AnyObject conformance makes the protocol Sendable across actors automatically
Because protocols cannot be used as property types without a class constraint
Because weak requires a reference type, and AnyObject rules out value-type conformers
Because Objective-C interop always requires an explicit AnyObject constraint

questions.prompt: How many total strong references to the Item instance exist right after this code runs, before anything is set to nil?
questions.explanation: `a` holds one strong reference, and appending it to `list` creates a second, independent strong reference to the very same instance — arrays store references to class instances, not copies of them.

options.text: One — appending to an array doesn't create a new reference, just an index
Two — one from the variable a, one from the array's element storage
Zero — the if-let creates a temporary copy, and the original a is unaffected
Three — one from a, one from the array, and one held internally by ARC's bookkeeping

questions.prompt: In the classic delegate pattern, the delegate-owning object holds its delegate as `weak var delegate: SomeDelegate?`. Why weak rather than strong?
questions.explanation: The delegating object (say, a data source) is typically owned by the delegate itself, or by something the delegate also owns. If the data source held its delegate strongly, the two would retain each other for as long as either exists — a cycle. Weak lets the data source refer to its delegate without contributing to that reference's lifetime.

options.text: Because delegate protocols cannot be marked class-only in Swift
Because a strong delegate reference would make the delegate's methods run synchronously
Because Objective-C requires weak delegates but Swift does not
Because the delegate typically already owns the delegating object

questions.prompt: A C callback stores a Swift object with Unmanaged.passUnretained, and a cleanup function later calls takeRetainedValue() on it exactly once. What's the problem?
questions.explanation: passUnretained doesn't add any retain of its own — it just wraps the pointer. takeRetainedValue, however, assumes it's consuming a +1 retain and releases one on top of reading the value. Since no matching retain was ever added, this releases one reference too many, which can deallocate the object early or corrupt memory.

options.text: passUnretained added no retain, but takeRetainedValue releases one anyway — an over-release
This is the correct, balanced pairing for passing an object across a C boundary
The object leaks, since neither call ever releases the reference passUnretained created
Unmanaged wrappers are read-only, so takeRetainedValue silently does nothing here

questions.prompt: An object's retain count reaches zero while your app is in the middle of a method call on a completely unrelated object. When does deinit run?
questions.explanation: ARC deallocation isn't deferred to idle time or the next run loop pass — it happens synchronously, the instant the last strong reference is released, wherever that happens to occur in your code.

options.text: At the next iteration of the main run loop
Only after the current call stack fully unwinds back to the top level
Immediately, at the exact point the last strong reference is released
The next time the app receives a memory warning

questions.prompt: A tight loop creates thousands of temporary Objective-C-bridged objects per iteration and is observed to hold peak memory far higher than expected until the loop finishes. What's the most likely fix?
questions.explanation: Objects an API hands back as autoreleased sit in the current autorelease pool until it drains, which normally happens once per run-loop iteration. Wrapping the loop body in its own autoreleasepool { } block drains those temporaries far more often, capping the peak instead of letting thousands accumulate.

options.text: Switch every bridged object from a class to a struct to avoid ARC entirely
Wrap the loop body in an explicit autoreleasepool { } to drain temporaries more frequently
Mark the loop variable weak so temporaries deallocate as soon as they're created
Add [unowned self] to the loop closure to stop it from retaining the enclosing context
